Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

thank you phrase

also thank you so much, I’m deeply grateful, I am deeply grateful to you, thanks very much, many thanks, thanks, I’m much obliged to you, I’m very grateful, thanks for sending, thanks!, thanks a lot, thanks a million, thanks a lot for, thank you (for a favour done)

classical

Traupman 109, 393
Plaut.

Amō tē.

thank you, for a kindness done

The idiom of Cicero’s letters.

Other words

  • Multum tē amō. — thank you so much

    also used · classical · Traupman 109, 393

  • Grātiam habeō (maximam). — thank you, I’m most grateful

    grātiam habēre alicui, to feel gratitude; grātiās agere is to say thank you formally · also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 5.8.61: bene fēcistī; grātiam habeō maximam (Lewis & Short), s.v. bene; Ter. Ad. 5.9.14: omnibus grātiam habeō (Lewis & Short), s.v. sēorsus; Traupman 99: tibi grātiam habeō maximam; Traupman 323

  • Fēcistī mihi pergrātum. — you have done me a great kindness: I’m much obliged to you

    pergrātum, neuter, “a very welcome thing”; what was done follows with quod and the indicative · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 2.4.1: fēcistī mihi pergrātum, quod Serāpiōnis librum ad mē mīsistī (Lewis & Short s.v. quod); Traupman 105: I’m much obliged to you for sending me your book, fēcistī mihi pergrātum quod librum ad mē mīsistī

    The letter-writer’s thanks: English thanks “for” something, Latin says what was done in a quod clause. In the future, as a request: grātum mihi fēceris sī ….

  • Maximās tibi grātiās agō. — thank you very much

    grātiās agere, to give thanks, with the person in the dative · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 13.24.2: tibi maximās grātiās agō (Lewis & Short s.v. grātia); Traupman 17: thanks a lot!, grātiās maximās!

    Formal thanks, as in a letter; face to face comedy says Amō tē or Grātiam habeō.

  • Grātiās! — thanks!

    also used · modern · Traupman 15, 17: thanks!, grātiās!; Traupman 55: grātiās tibi; Traupman 56: multās grātiās!, thanks a lot; Traupman 173: grātiās multās!, thanks a lot; Traupman 393

    We have found no classical instance without agere (Lewis & Short quotes it only with the verb), but it is used so in modern Latin; the classical forms are grātiās agō and grātiam habeō. Traupman 17 also gives grātiās maximās!, thanks a lot, and sescentās grātiās!, thanks a million (sescentī, six hundred, is the comic “countless”: Plaut. Trin. 3.3.62, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • «Bene factum,» inquit avia. «Amō tē.»

    “Well done,” said Grandma. “Thank you.”composed

See also please, give thanks.
